transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-16
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sam Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (Pioneer Trust CISO), Aisha Rahman (Pioneer Trust Security Manager), Ethan Cole (Procurement)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of the customer's SIG questionnaire, clarifying evidence items for SOC 2/ISO, RBAC/SSO, audit logging, data residency, and KMS. Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide redacted SOC 2, SIG answers, and KMS diagram; follow-up evidence review next week.

[00:00] Sam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sam Lee from Redwood, this is Priya Nair, our security/solutions engineer. Should we do a quick roll call?
[00:08] Michael: Michael here, CISO at Pioneer Trust. Thanks for doing this. We have Aisha and Ethan on as well.
[00:15] Aisha: Hi, thanks.
[00:17] Ethan: Hey all.
[00:20] Priya: Great. The goal for today is to walk through the SIG questions you highlighted and call out where we'll need evidence or architecture artifacts - SOC 2 type II, encryption and KMS, SSO, RBAC, audit logs, sub-processors, that kind of thing.
[00:34] Michael: Yep exactly. We've got some internal auditors who want redwood's responses. We also have a vendor risk team that wants to know whether your hosted API will keep data in-region, and how keys are managed if we go with Redwood Private.
[00:47] Sam: Perfect. To be clear we support three deployment modes - hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For most SIG items the answers are similar but we'll call out differences.
[00:58] Aisha: Let's start with SOC 2 and evidence. We need a redacted SOC 2 Type II report and can you confirm scope - is inference tier and console included?
[01:08] Priya: Yes. Redwood's SOC 2 scope covers the hosted control plane and inference runtime for the managed service; dedicated customers have separate attestations for reserved capacity contracts - for Private deployments we provide SOC2 attestation for the control plane operations and provide guidance for customer-managed infrastructure. We'll share a redacted SOC2 report and a mapping doc showing controls in scope.
[01:30] Michael: When you say "mapping doc," do you map the SOC2 controls to the SIG questions? Our team prefers that.
[01:36] Priya: Yes, we'll include a SOC2-to-SIG mapping spreadsheet showing control IDs and the relevant evidence artifacts.
[01:42] Ethan: Good. For evidence, are you able to share penetration test reports or vulnerability scan summaries?
[01:48] Sam: We can share executive summaries of external pentests and a vulnerability management overview; full raw reports are sensitive but we can provide attestation and remediation timelines and redacted proofs.
[01:58] Aisha: Next: SSO and RBAC. We need SAML 2.0/Okta integration details, can users be scoped to roles?
[02:05] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports SAML 2.0 and OIDC; we have first-class Okta integrations and can map SAML attributes to RBAC roles. Our RBAC model supports orgs, teams, and route-level permissions. We'll provide the SAML metadata, an example assertion, and admin role documentation.
[02:22] Michael: How does role change propagate? If an engineer is removed from Okta, how soon does access revoke in Redwood?
[02:28] Priya: We honor standard SAML session behavior; we also recommend SCIM provisioning for faster deprovisioning. With SCIM, deprovisioning in Okta propagates within seconds to minutes depending on your IdP polling.
[02:40] Michael: SCIM is required for us ideally.
[02:43] Priya: Noted - we'll flag SCIM as recommended and include how to enable it.
[02:49] Ethan: On audit logging - we need immutable audit logs, retention options, and the ability to stream logs to our SIEM.
[02:56] Priya: Redwood Console logs admin actions, API calls, model deployments, and inference requests at the metadata level. We keep immutable logs for a default retention window and can extend retention as an enterprise add-on. Logs can be exported to S3, or streamed via secure syslog/HTTPS to your SIEM. We'll share the audit log schema and sample events.
[03:12] Aisha: You said "inference requests at the metadata level" - can you clarify what you log vs store full request payloads?
[03:18] Sam: By default we log metadata and traces - timestamps, model, route, token usage and latency, and redaction markers. Customer content is not retained in plaintext unless you opt in; hosted API has configurable retention, and Private deployments default to customer data staying in their VPC. We'll include retention policy docs.
[03:38] Michael: That's helpful. For regulatory reasons we need data residency - can you guarantee data stays within a specific region or country for hosted deployments?
[03:47] Priya: We have region pins for hosted customers - requests can be routed to a regional cluster. However the control plane might still be in a global control region; for strict residency we recommend Redwood Private or a Dedicated deployment with regional commitments. We'll include the exact routing and region guarantees in the SLA appendix.
[04:04] Michael: OK. Next: encryption and KMS. How do you manage customer keys - BYOK? HSM?
[04:10] Priya: Good question. For hosted we offer platform-managed keys (encryption at rest with cloud KMS) and a BYOK/HSM option for Enterprise: you can bring keys via Cloud KMS or use an external HSM with customer-managed keys. For Private deployments, customers manage keys entirely in their environment. We'll provide a KMS architecture diagram and the key rotation policy.
[04:30] Aisha: Does Redwood ever have access to customer plaintext if using BYOK?
[04:34] Priya: No, with a proper BYOK flow Redwood only sees encrypted blobs. For certain operational needs we have procedures to request emergency access but they're governed by policy and require multi-party approvals; we'll include that in the AUP (acceptable use policy) and the DPIA.
[04:48] Ethan: Are logs that contain user identifiers encrypted?
[04:51] Priya: Yes, logs are encrypted at rest. Sensitive fields are redacted in the UI; for SIEM export we can provide hashed or tokenized identifiers per your preference.
[05:00] Sam: A small note - sometimes the transcript text will say KV cash instead of KV cache, so apologies for any transcription artifacts.
[05:06] Michael: (laughs) noted.
[05:08] Michael: On subprocessors - we need your subprocessor list and SSAE/SOC2 coverage for those providers.
[05:14] Sam: We'll provide the current subprocessor list and for major vendors we'll indicate where they fall under our SOC2 coverage or separate attestations.
[05:21] Aisha: The SIG has a bunch of odd controls about change management and backdoor detection; can you map your CI/CD and release process?
[05:29] Priya: Yes: we run code reviews, CI with security gates, automated scanning, and a staged rollout for runtime changes. For inference kernels we have a kernel review and verification step; we'll include the change management doc and a sample deployment timeline.
[05:44] Michael: Do you perform red team or adversarial model checks?
[05:48] Priya: We do internal model safety checks, prompt safety filters at the API layer, and periodic external audits for the runtime. For customers that need stricter controls we can include additional model guardrails as part of the Dedicated/Private offering.
[06:01] Ethan: One procurement question - if we go with Redwood Dedicated versus Redwood Private, what security artifacts differ?
[06:08] Sam: Dedicated: Redwood manages the GPU pool in dedicated tenants; we provide SOC2 and network diagrams, and you get stricter tenancy isolation plus guaranteed throughput. Private: customers manage the networking and can host the runtime in their VPC or on-prem. Evidence wise, Private has more customer-provided artifacts (since infra is customer-owned) but Redwood provides control plane attestations and runbooks.
[06:26] Michael: Great. There are a few SIG items where we asked for "evidence of implementation" like MFA enforcement and vulnerability scanning cadence - can you confirm MFA across admin accounts?
[06:36] Priya: Yes, MFA enforced for admin consoles; API keys can be scoped and rotated. Vulnerability scans are weekly internal and monthly external scans; critical findings have a defined SLA for remediation. We'll provide a vulnerability management summary and a sample scan digest.
[06:52] Aisha: For legal, our team will want a DPA and subprocessor clause prior to pilot.
[06:57] Sam: We'll share our standard DPA and are open to negotiation at enterprise scale.
[07:01] Ethan: For evidence delivery, what's the preferred method? We prefer a secure file share or SFTP.
[07:06] Sam: We'll put the artifacts in a secure Redwood Shared link with time-limited access; if you need SFTP we can coordinate with security.
[07:14] Michael: OK, last question - do you provide attestations for ISO 27001?
[07:18] Priya: We're in progress on ISO 27001 certification; we can share the current gap assessment and timeline for certification. SOC2 Type II is available now.
[07:27] Sam: To recap next steps: we'll upload redacted SOC2, completed SIG answers, KMS diagram, SAML/SCIM docs, audit log schema, and subprocessor list. Then schedule a follow-up to go through the evidence.
[07:41] Michael: Sounds good. Aim to get the documents to us by Friday.
[07:44] Sam: We'll target 2026-12-18.
[07:46] Aisha: Thanks, appreciate it.
[07:48] Priya: One more note - for the SIG spreadsheet there are a couple items where we'll answer "partial" or "depends on deployment mode" - we'll flag those and include clarifying notes.
[07:58] Michael: Perfect. That's all from my side.
[08:00] Ethan: Thanks everyone.
[08:02] Sam: Thanks - we'll follow up with links and a calendar invite for the evidence review.
[08:06] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed as "KV cash"), filler words and overlap. The transcript above has been lightly edited for readability but preserves conversational turns and key timestamps.
